umare.title: Born to One's Station → Rising in the World → Self-Responsibility → Parent Gacha
umare.lead: Status in early-modern Japan was decided by birth. Meiji proclamations took the privileges off the samurai, and the Education System Order preached making one's way through learning. In 2004 "self-responsibility" was turned on the hostages; in 2021 "parent gacha" made the top ten of the buzzword award. Set in order of date, 150 years of denying birth come back to a word for lamenting it.
umare.spanLabel: From the status edicts to the buzzword

inkyo.title: Inkyo Retirement → FIRE
inkyo.lead: Inkyo was the standard life plan of early-modern Japan. The Meiji Civil Code made it a legal act, requiring as a rule that the house head be 60 or over. In 1948 the articles went, and the time to step back came to be decided by the mandatory retirement age. In 2020 it came back as an acronym born in the United States.

shudo.title: Shudo → Diversity
shudo.lead: Society has rewritten the treatment of relations between men again and again, each time under a different label. Early-modern shudo was spoken of openly as the bond of an older man and a youth; in the first years of Meiji sodomy became punishable; in the Taisho years it was called "perversion". The American Psychiatric Association dropped homosexuality as a diagnosis in 1973 and the WHO in 1990, and in 2015 a ward office issued certificates to same-sex couples.
shudo.spanLabel: From the penal article to the certificate

nodes.note: The WHO followed in 1990.

nodes.label: Diversity
nodes.note: Partnership certificates. The Understanding Promotion Act in 2023.

kekkon.title: Romantic Love → Arranged Marriage → Love-Marriage Ideal → Konkatsu
kekkon.lead: The first use of renai in Japanese is in a translated book of 1870. Seven in ten of the couples who married in the 1930s married by miai, and the love match took the lead only with the marriages of 1965-69. Love marriage, which rose to nearly nine in ten in the 2000s, is being closed on, among the marriages of 2019-21, by couples who met "online".
kekkon.spanLabel: From a translated word to meeting online

mottainai.title: Mottainai → MOTTAINAI
mottainai.lead: In A Collection of Tales from Uji, of the Kamakura period, the word is used in the sense of "improper"; in the Taiheiki of the 14th century it is also used of regret at waste. In 2005 a Kenyan environmental activist proposed at the United Nations that it be spread to the world, and in 2019 the Act on Promotion of Food Loss and Waste Reduction, which calls for fostering an awareness of not wasting food, came into force.
mottainai.spanLabel: From Tales from Uji to the UN speech

mujo.title: Impermanence → Mindfulness
mujo.lead: Meditation on impermanence lies at the core of Buddhism. In 1979 it became a medical programme at an American medical school, in 2007 an in-house course at Google, and in 2016 an NHK Special took it up as a way of coping with stress. It is not the direct descendant of the impermanence of medieval literature but the same Buddhist practice, come back by way of the United States.

nodes.label: Impermanence

hataraku.title: Diligence as Virtue → Guts → Fight 24 Hours? → Work-Life Balance
hataraku.lead: Not a line of descent but norms of work that have replaced one another in the same place, set in order of date: the conventional morality of the late Edo period, the guts of the Tokyo Olympics, a commercial jingle of 1989, a charter of 2007.

koyo.title: Many Jobs at Once → Lifetime Employment → Side Jobs Allowed
koyo.lead: In the pre-modern village a good many households kept trade or a craft alongside farming. Abegglen called Japanese employment a lifetime commitment. The next year, 1959, employees passed half of all persons in employment. In 2018 the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare struck the ban on side jobs from its Model Rules of Employment.

ko.title: Mutual Aid Circles → Crowdfunding
ko.lead: Tanomoshi-ko appears in a document of 1275. Mujin was put under licence by statute in 1915, mujin companies became sogo banks in 1951, and in 1989 52 sogo banks converted to ordinary banks. Crowdfunding began in Japan with a purchase-type service in 2011. It is not a direct descendant of the ko but a similar product from a different factory.

shiken.title: Imperial Exams → Rising in the World → Credentialism → Red over Expert
shiken.lead: Choosing people by examination rather than by birth begins in China in 598. It ran for 1,300 years, stopped with a single edict on 2 September 1905, and came back in 1952 as the gaokao. Japan's Education System Order of 1872 preached that "learning is the capital by which one makes one's way", and the phrase "credential society" settled in during the 1960s. In China, for eleven and a half years after 1966, university entrance had no examination at all.
shiken.spanLabel: From the edict of 598 to the return of the exam

shoyu.title: Serfdom → Bound by Indenture → Slavery in Brazil → Slaveholding as Lawful
shoyu.lead: The premise that a person can be owned ended on a different date in each country. Russia by the emancipation manifesto of 1861, Japan by Grand Council Proclamation No. 295 of 1872, Brazil by the Golden Law of 1888, Saudi Arabia in 1962. In every case a single piece of legislation ended it, and the text is short. The Golden Law has two articles.
shoyu.spanLabel: From the Russian manifesto to the Saudi abolition

karada.title: Blackened Teeth → The Queue → Foot Binding
karada.en: The State Comes for the Body
karada.lead: Modernisation reached the look of the body first. Japan stopped the blackening of teeth and the shaving of brows for the nobility in 1870, and the order of the following year allowed the topknot to be cut. In China the queue, which in 1645 you died for not shaving, became unlawful to keep on 5 March 1912. Eight days later came the order against foot binding. In each case a single proclamation ended a custom of the body.
karada.spanLabel: From the 1870 order to the cutting of queues

ie.title: The House Name First → The Hoju System
ie.lead: Japan's house system became law in the Meiji Civil Code of 1898 and was gone between 1947 and 1948. In between, on 1 July 1923, the Government-General of Korea amended the Korean Civil Ordinance and put the Japanese household register into force. The transplanted house system outlived the country that made it: it was abolished on 1 January 2008, sixty years after Japan let it go.

sanseiken.title: Politics Is for Men → No Vote for Women
sanseiken.lead: New Zealand was the first country to let women vote, in 1893. In Japan, article 5 of the Public Order and Police Act of 1900 barred women from political associations; "women" stood in the same list as soldiers and police. It was repealed on 21 November 1945. The Swiss federal constitution said "every Swiss" and did not mean women, and the federal court twice gave custom as the reason. It was settled by the referendum of 7 February 1971.

taibatsu.title: Smacking Children → Discipline by Force
taibatsu.lead: A parent's right to hit a child was not merely custom; it had the law behind it. In Japan corporal punishment in schools was forbidden in 1879, while the right to chastise at home became article 882 of the Meiji Civil Code in 1898. The home outlasted the school. Sweden was the first country to forbid it outright, home included, on 1 July 1979; Japan deleted article 822 on 16 December 2022.
